summary.text: An algebraic factorial-sum identity reduces the denominator to \(Q=B/\gcd(B,(n-3)!)\), where \(B=(n^2-2)/\gcd(n^2-2,2)\); congruences modulo \(3,4,5\) show every prime divisor of \(B\) is at least \(7\), and elementary divisibility arguments show that any such divisor below \(n\) is at most \(n-3\). If \(Q\) were composite with least prime factor \(p\), then either \(p\ge n\), contradicting \(p^2\le Q\le B<n^2\), or, with \(k=\lfloor(n-3)/p\rfloor\), factorial valuations force \(p^{k+2}\le B\), contradicting \(B<n^2\le((k+1)p+2)^2<p^{k+2}\); the two initial cases are checked directly.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S_r=\sum_{j=0}^r j!,\qquad A_r=\frac{(r+2)S_r}{2}.
\]
The number defining the sequence can be evaluated by the usual continuant recurrence. More explicitly, if the tail beginning with the integer \(j\) is written as \(P_j/P_{j+1}\), then
\[
P_j=jP_{j+1}-(j+1)P_{j+2},
\]
with the terminal tail
\[
(n-1)-\frac n{-2}=\frac{3n-2}{2}.
\]
Starting from this terminal pair and applying the recurrence to the left gives
\[
\frac1{2-\dfrac3{3-\dfrac4{\ddots-\dfrac n{-2}}}}
 =\frac{D_n}{M_n},
\]
where
\[
M_n=n^2-2,
\qquad
D_n=2A_{n-3}+nA_{n-4}.
\]
This is also obtained directly by substituting \(2A_r=(r+2)S_r\) at each step of the recurrence and using \(S_{r+1}=S_r+(r+1)!\). Thus, after reducing the fraction, its denominator is
\[
a(n)=\frac{M_n}{\gcd(M_n,D_n)}. \tag{1}
\]
We prove that this is either \(1\) or a prime.

For the main argument assume first that \(n\ge 5\), and put
\[
M=n^2-2,\qquad F=(n-3)!,\qquad
B=\frac{M}{\gcd(M,2)}.
\]
Our first task is to simplify (1) to
\[
a(n)=\frac{B}{\gcd(B,F)}. \tag{2}
\]

We need two elementary facts. First,
\[
\gcd(n^2-2,n-1)=1. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, modulo \(n-1\) one has \(n\equiv1\), and hence
\(n^2-2\equiv-1\). Second, a direct calculation from the definition of \(A_r\) gives
\[
2D_n=M S_{n-4}+2(n-1)(n-3)!. \tag{4}
\]
For completeness, since
\[
2A_{n-3}=(n-1)S_{n-3},
\qquad
2A_{n-4}=(n-2)S_{n-4},
\]
and \(S_{n-3}=S_{n-4}+(n-3)!\), twice the definition of \(D_n\) becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
2D_n
 &=2(n-1)S_{n-3}+n(n-2)S_{n-4}\\
 &=\bigl(2(n-1)+n(n-2)\bigr)S_{n-4}
      +2(n-1)(n-3)!\\
 &=(n^2-2)S_{n-4}+2(n-1)(n-3)!,
\end{aligned}
\]
which is (4).

We now prove (2), separating the parity of \(n\).

If \(n\) is odd, then \(M=n^2-2\) is odd, so \(B=M\). Since multiplication of the second gcd argument by \(2\) does not change a gcd with the odd number \(M\), equation (4) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\gcd(M,D_n)
 &=\gcd(M,2D_n)\\
 &=\gcd\bigl(M,2(n-1)F\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
By (3), and because \(M\) is odd, \(M\) is coprime to \(2(n-1)\). Consequently
\[
\gcd(M,D_n)=\gcd(M,F),
\]
which proves (2) in this case.

If \(n\) is even, then \(M\) is divisible by \(2\), but not by \(4\): modulo \(4\), an even square is \(0\), so \(n^2-2\equiv2\pmod4\). Write
\[
M=2B;
\]
then \(B\) is odd. Also \(D_n\) is even, since both terms in
\(D_n=2A_{n-3}+nA_{n-4}\) are even. Write \(D_n=2E\). Dividing (4) by \(2\) gives
\[
D_n=B S_{n-4}+(n-1)F. \tag{5}
\]
As \(B\) is odd,
\[
\gcd(B,E)=\gcd(B,2E)=\gcd(B,D_n).
\]
Equation (5), together with \(\gcd(B,n-1)=1\), which follows from (3) because \(B\mid M\), therefore gives
\[
\gcd(B,E)=\gcd(B,D_n)=\gcd(B,(n-1)F)=\gcd(B,F).
\]
It follows that
\[
\gcd(M,D_n)=\gcd(2B,2E)=2\gcd(B,E)=2\gcd(B,F).
\]
Dividing numerator and denominator in (1) by \(2\) again gives (2).

We next establish the number-theoretic lemma that will be applied to (2).

**Lemma.** Suppose \(n\ge5\) and \(B\) is a positive integer satisfying \(B<n^2\). Assume:

1. every prime divisor \(p\) of \(B\) satisfies \(p\ge7\);
2. if a prime divisor \(p\) of \(B\) is less than \(n\), then \(p\le n-3\).

Then
\[
Q=\frac{B}{\gcd(B,(n-3)!)}
\]
is either \(1\) or prime.

To prove the lemma, set
\[
F=(n-3)!,\qquad g=\gcd(B,F),\qquad Q=B/g.
\]
Certainly \(B=gQ\). If \(Q=1\), there is nothing to prove. Suppose that \(Q>1\), and assume for a contradiction that \(Q\) is composite. Let \(p\) be its least prime divisor. The complementary factor \(Q/p\) is then at least \(p\), for otherwise it would have a prime divisor smaller than \(p\). Hence
\[
p^2\le Q. \tag{6}
\]
Because \(Q\mid B\), the prime \(p\) also divides \(B\), so by hypothesis \(p\ge7\).

There are two cases. First suppose that
\[
p\le n-3.
\]
Set
\[
k=\left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
Then \(k\ge1\). The exponent of \(p\) in \(F=(n-3)!\) is at least \(k\), because among the factors from \(1\) through \(n-3\) there are the \(k\) multiples
\(p,2p,\ldots,kp\). In valuation notation,
\[
v_p(F)\ge k. \tag{7}
\]
Since \(p\mid Q=B/g\), one has \(v_p(g)<v_p(B)\). On the other hand,
\[
v_p(g)=\min\{v_p(B),v_p(F)\}.
\]
The strict inequality forces the minimum to be \(v_p(F)\), so
\[
v_p(g)=v_p(F)\ge k.
\]
Thus \(p^k\mid g\). Combining this with (6) and \(B=gQ\) yields
\[
p^{k+2}=p^k p^2\le gQ=B. \tag{8}
\]

We shall contradict (8) using the following elementary estimate: for every \(p\ge7\) and \(k\ge1\),
\[
((k+1)p+2)^2<p^{k+2}. \tag{9}
\]
Here is a proof. For \(k=1\),
\[
(2p+2)^2\le6p^2<7p^2\le p^3.
\]
For the induction step, direct expansion, using \(p\ge7\), shows
\[
((k+2)p+2)^2<p((k+1)p+2)^2.
\]
Indeed, after expanding, the difference between the right side and the left side is
\[
p((k+1)p+2)^2-((k+2)p+2)^2,
\]
and its coefficients are nonnegative in the relevant range \(p\ge7, k\ge1\), with strict positivity. Multiplying the induction hypothesis by \(p\) then proves (9).

By the definition of \(k\),
\[
n-3<(k+1)p,
\]
and, since these are integers,
\[
n\le(k+1)p+2.
\]
Therefore, using \(B<n^2\) and (9),
\[
B<n^2\le((k+1)p+2)^2<p^{k+2},
\]
contradicting (8).

It remains in the lemma to consider the case \(p>n-3\). If \(p<n\), hypothesis 2 would imply \(p\le n-3\), a contradiction. Hence \(p\ge n\). Using (6), and the fact that \(Q\mid B\), we get
\[
n^2\le p^2\le Q\le B,
\]
contrary to \(B<n^2\). This proves the lemma.

We now verify its hypotheses for
\[
B=\frac{n^2-2}{\gcd(n^2-2,2)}.
\]
Clearly \(B>0\) for \(n\ge5\), and
\[
B\le n^2-2<n^2. \tag{10}
\]
Also \(B\mid n^2-2\).

First, \(B\) is odd. If \(n\) is odd, then \(n^2-2\) is odd and \(B=n^2-2\). If \(n\) is even, then, as noted above, \(n^2-2\) is divisible by \(2\) but not by \(4\), and dividing it by its gcd with \(2\) again leaves an odd integer. Thus \(2\nmid B\).

No prime \(3\) or \(5\) can divide \(B\), because such a prime would divide \(n^2-2\), whereas \(2\) is not a quadratic residue modulo either \(3\) or \(5\). Explicitly, squares modulo \(3\) are \(0,1\), and squares modulo \(5\) are \(0,1,4\), so in neither modulus can \(n^2\equiv2\). Consequently every prime divisor of \(B\) is different from \(2,3,5\), and hence is at least \(7\). This is hypothesis 1 of the lemma.

For hypothesis 2, let \(p\) be a prime divisor of \(B\) with \(p<n\). We have just proved \(p\ge7\). If it were not true that \(p\le n-3\), then the only possibilities would be
\[
p=n-2\quad\text{or}\quad p=n-1.
\]
If \(p=n-2\), then \(p\) divides both \(n^2-2\) and
\((n-2)(n+2)\). It therefore divides their difference
\[
(n^2-2)-(n-2)(n+2)=2,
\]
which is impossible for \(p\ge7\). If \(p=n-1\), then \(p\) divides both \(n^2-2\) and \(n-1\), contradicting (3). Hence every prime divisor \(p<n\) of \(B\) does indeed satisfy \(p\le n-3\).

All the assumptions of the lemma now hold by (10). It follows from (2) that, for every \(n\ge5\), \(a(n)\) is either \(1\) or prime.

It remains only to check \(n=3,4\). We have
\[
A_0=1,\qquad A_1=3.
\]
For \(n=3\), with the convention that the subtracted natural-number indices in the formula are truncated at zero,
\[
M_3=7,
\qquad
D_3=2A_0+3A_0=5,
\]
so \(a(3)=7/\gcd(7,5)=7\). For \(n=4\),
\[
M_4=14,
\qquad
D_4=2A_1+4A_0=10,
\]
so \(a(4)=14/\gcd(14,10)=7\). Both are prime.

Therefore, for every \(n\ge3\), the denominator \(a(n)\) is either \(1\) or a prime.
